### [Prelims Source Page 154](pages/prelims/prelims_page_154.pdf)

CONSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK
Part XV at a glance (Arts 324 to 329)
- Art 324: Election Commission of India; superintendence, direction and control of electoral rolls and of elections to
Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice President.
- Art 325: One general electoral roll per constituency; no one excluded only on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex;
no separate communal electorates.
- Art 326: Adult suffrage; every citizen aged 18+ who is not disqualified may be registered. Age lowered from 21 to 18
by the 61st Amendment, 1988.
- Arts 327, 328: Parliament legislates on all election matters (used for the RPA, 1950 and RPA, 1951); the State
Legislature only where Parliament has not. Both are “subject to the provisions of this Constitution”.
- Art 329: Bar on courts: (a) laws on delimitation and seat allotment; (b) elections questioned only by election
petition.
Traps
- Part XV has no article on political parties. Parties got constitutional mention only in the Tenth Schedule (52nd
Amendment, 1985), which defines “legislature party” and “original political party” but not “political party”.
- Local body elections are outside Part XV; State Election Commissions run them (Arts 243K, 243ZA).
- Art 325 lists only religion, race, caste and sex; place of birth, descent and residence are not in it, and the RPA, 1950
requires ordinary residence.
- Art 326 applies only to the Lok Sabha and Assemblies, not to indirectly elected bodies (Rajya Sabha, Councils,
President, Vice President). Vote at 18, contest at 25.
- The voting age came by the 61st, not the 62nd Amendment (which extended SC/ST and Anglo-Indian reservation).
- State Assemblies to formulate election laws only in so far as Parliament has not already made a provision on the
matter.
Election Commission of India (Art 324)
- Composition: The CEC and such number of Election Commissioners as the President fixes; three members at
present, but the Constitution fixes no number.
- Appointment: By the President on the recommendation of a Selection Committee of the Prime Minister, a Union
Cabinet Minister and the Leader of the Opposition (CEC and other ECs Act, 2023).
- Removal: The CEC only like a Supreme Court Judge; other ECs only on the CEC’s recommendation (Art 324(5)).
- Reservoir of power: Acts where the law is silent (Mohinder Singh Gill, 1978): by elections, symbols, party
recognition, Model Code of Conduct, observers, countermanding a poll.
- Limit: Cannot act contrary to existing law. In A.C. Jose v Sivan Pillai (1984), EVMs used without statutory backing
were set aside, so Parliament had to legislate.
Traps
- Outside the ECI: panchayat and municipal polls (SECs), the election of the Speaker/Deputy Speaker, and
nominated Rajya Sabha members.
- The Ministry of Home Affairs has no role in fixing the election schedule; it is the ECI alone.
ECI versus State Election Commission (Arts 243K, 243ZA)
- SEC: Created by the 73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992; appointed by the Governor; conducts panchayat and
municipal rolls and elections.
- Protection: The SEC is removable only like a High Court Judge, and his service conditions cannot be varied to his
disadvantage; the CEC is protected like a Supreme Court Judge.
Traps
- The SEC is wholly independent of the ECI; the ECI has no supervisory or appellate role over it.
- The State Election Commissioner sits ex officio on the Delimitation Commission for his State (Delimitation Act,
2002).

### [Prelims Source Page 155](pages/prelims/prelims_page_155.pdf)

THE TWO REPRESENTATION OF THE PEOPLE ACTS
How to tell the two Acts apart
- The RPA, 1950 builds the stage: who may vote, the electoral roll, and how many seats each State has.
- The RPA, 1951 runs the play: qualifications and disqualifications, party registration, nomination, polling, corrupt
practices, results and election petitions.
- Where an item is constitutional, the Act supplies the machinery.
- Party registration entered the law only in 1989, through the RPA, 1951; the RPA, 1950 nowhere mentions political
parties.
Trap: The Model Code of Conduct, party symbols, NOTA, electoral bonds belong to neither Act.
SEATS AND DELIMITATION
Allocation of seats (RPA, 1950)
- State wise seats in the Lok Sabha (First Schedule), Assemblies (Second Schedule) and Councils (Third Schedule),
with SC/ST reserved seats and the manner of filling Council seats.
- The ceilings come from the Constitution (Art 81 for the Lok Sabha, Art 170 for Assemblies); the distribution among
States comes from the Act.
Traps
- Rajya Sabha seats are allotted in the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution, not the RPA.
Delimitation Commission (Delimitation Act, 2002)
- Members: A serving or retired Supreme Court Judge (Chairperson, appointed by the Centre); the CEC or an EC
nominated by him; and the State Election Commissioner of the State concerned (both ex officio).
- Associate members (MPs and MLAs of the State) assist but have no vote and sign no decision.
- Orders are published in the Gazette and laid before the Lok Sabha and the Assembly concerned (Sec 10); they apply
from the next general election. The ECI keeps them updated for minor corrections under the RPA, 1950.
Traps
- The Commission is statutory, unlike the ECI and the Finance Commission.
- Orders have the force of law: legislatures cannot modify them and courts cannot question them (Art 329(a);
Meghraj Kothari, 1967), except where delimitation is manifestly arbitrary (Kishorchandra Rathod, 2024).
Delimitation exercises so far [PRELIMS 2024]
- Four Commissions: 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002 (under the Acts of 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002).
- The 2002 Commission (Justice Kuldip Singh) finalised its orders in 2008, leaving out J&K, Assam, Arunachal
Pradesh, Manipur and Nagaland.
- Two later exercises, not Commissions under Art 82:
- J&K: Under the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019; 90 Assembly seats (43 Jammu, 47 Kashmir).
- Assam: By the ECI under the RPA, 1950; 126 Assembly and 14 Lok Sabha seats kept.
Traps
- The count stays at four; the J&K and Assam exercises do not add to it.
Women’s reservation (106th Amendment, 2023)
- Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam: Inserted Arts 330A, 332A and a proviso to Art 239AA(2)(b); one third of seats in
the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Delhi Assembly, including within SC/ST reserved seats, for 15 years.
- In force from 16 April 2026, but reservation applies only after delimitation following the first census taken after
commencement.
Traps
- Constitutional but not yet operational; the 131st Amendment Bill, 2026, which sought to advance it, was defeated.
- Rajya Sabha and Councils are excluded; there is no OBC sub quota.

The 2026 delimitation package
- The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, the Delimitation Bill and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment)
Bill were introduced on 16 April 2026: to lift the freeze, let Parliament decide by law when delimitation is done and
on which census, and raise the Lok Sabha ceiling from 550 to 850 (States 530 to 815, UTs 20 to 35).
- Defeated on 17 April 2026: 298 of 528 present and voting, short of the two thirds required by Art 368(2); 230
against. The Delimitation Bill was then withdrawn.
Traps
- The freeze until the first census after 2026 still stands.

- Registration is not voting: a convict stays an elector, so he can propose a candidate and contest (subject to Sec 8),
but cannot vote while confined.
- A non member Minister can speak in either House (Arts 88, 177) but cannot vote.

Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
- The ECI’s door to door reverification by Booth Level Officers (BLOs), followed by a draft roll and claims and
objections; deletions are recorded under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. Legal basis: Art 324 and Sec
21(3), RPA 1950.
- Supreme Court (27 May 2026): A Bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi upheld the SIR. The ECI
may examine citizenship only for enrolment, not as a final declaration; Aadhaar is accepted as the 12th document,
for identity, not citizenship.
Traps
- The SIR revises the roll; it is not a citizenship determination.
Overseas (NRI) electors (RP (Amendment) Act, 2010)
- A citizen living abroad who has not acquired foreign citizenship registers at the address in his passport (Form 6A,
Sec 20A, RPA 1950).
- He must vote in person at his polling station in India.
Traps
- No postal ballot and no proxy; the 2018 Bill for NRI proxy voting lapsed.
- OCI and PIO cardholders cannot enrol, as they are not citizens.

Traps
- Only Classified Service Voters can use a proxy. The proxy’s ink goes on the left middle finger, so he can still cast his
own vote.
- NRIs get no postal ballot and no proxy.
- The absentee age is 85, raised from 80 in March 2024.
- Voters on election duty are not “absentee voters”, and special voters are often missed in lists.
- Preventive detainees can vote; convicts and undertrials cannot.
- ETPBS sends only the blank ballot electronically; the marked ballot returns by post.
- Service voters are listed in a separate part of their home constituency’s roll.
Constitutional Disqualifications (Arts 102, 191)
- Office of profit; unsound mind declared by a court; undischarged insolvent; not a citizen, or voluntarily acquired
foreign citizenship; disqualified by any law made by Parliament.
- Defection is a separate ground (Arts 102(2), 191(2); Tenth Schedule).
Traps
- Disqualification of a sitting member is decided by the President/Governor on the ECI’s opinion, which is binding
(Arts 103, 192).
- Defection goes to the Speaker/Chairman; the ECI has no role.
- Disqualifications under Arts 102, 191 are constitutional; those in the RPA are statutory.

Election Commission of India
ECI, established under Article 324 of the Constitution, oversees the electoral processes for Parliament, State
Legislatures, and the executive offices of the President and Vice-President.
Powers and Functions of ECI
Administrative Functions
1. Delimitation: Determines the territorial areas of electoral constituencies on the basis of the Delimitation
Commission Act.
2. Electoral Rolls: Prepares and periodically revises electoral rolls; registers all eligible voters.
3. Election Schedules: Notifies the dates and schedules of elections (General and By-elections).
4. Registration of Parties: Grants recognition to political parties and allots election symbols.
Advisory Functions
1. Disqualification: Advises the President and Governor on matters regarding the post-election
disqualification of Members of Parliament and MLAs respectively
2. President's Rule: Advises the President on whether elections can be held in a state under President's
Rule to extend the period of emergency after one year.
Quasi-Judicial Functions
1. Dispute Settlement: Acts as a court for settling disputes related to the granting of recognition to political
parties and the allotment of symbols.
2. Inquiry Officers: Appoints officers to inquire into disputes relating to electoral arrangements.
3. Expenditure Monitoring: Disqualifies candidates who fail to lodge their election expenses within the
time/manner set by law (Section 10A, RPA 1951).
Supervisory Functions
1. Model Code of Conduct (MCC): Ensures strict observance of the MCC by political parties and candidates
from the date of election announcement.
2. Monitoring Expenditure: Sets limits and monitors campaign spending to ensure a level playing field.
3. Poll Cancellation: Cancels polls in cases of booth capturing, rigging, violence, or other irregularities.
4. Supervision of Machinery: Directs and controls the entire election staff (including police and civil
servants) during the poll period.
Measures taken by ECI to strengthen the electoral process
1. Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) & Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT)
2. Model Code of Conduct (MCC): to ensure a level playing field, maintaining public order, and preventing
practices such as hate speech, vote-buying, and misuse of government resources.
3. ECINET (2026): Launched a "one-stop" digital interface integrating 40+ mobile and web applications to
provide a seamless experience for voters and officials.
4. 100% Webcasting: Mandated live webcasting from all polling stations (previously only "sensitive" ones)
to monitor critical poll-day activities in real-time.
5. Special Intensive Revision (SIR) 2025: Conducted a massive cleanup of electoral rolls across 12 States,
removing deceased voters and duplicate entries for over 51 crore electors.
6. cVIGIL App: Empowered citizens to report MCC violations; the ECI now mandates a 100-minute
turnaround time for investigators to respond.

The MCC is a set of non-statutory norms agreed upon by political parties to ensure "free and fair" elections
by preventing the ruling party from misusing state machinery and curbing unethical campaign practices.
Historical Evolution:

1. Duration: Becomes effective the moment the ECI announces the election schedule and remains in force
until the results are declared.

censure candidates, or delay polls. Criminal violations (bribery, hate speech) are prosecuted under the

before polling ends.

exit poll results from the commencement of the first phase of polling until half an hour after the close of
polling in the final phase.
3. Penalty: Violation of Section 126A is punishable by up to two years of imprisonment, a fine, or both.
4. Article 324: The Election Commission (ECI) uses its plenary powers to issue guidelines for print media
(which is not strictly covered by Sec 126) to ensure they don't publish polls during the prohibited
window.
Objectives of Opinion and Exit Polls
1. Voter Sentiment Mapping
2. Early Result Indication
3. Demographic Analysis
4. Issue Identification
5. Campaign Success Assessment
6. Democratic Engagement
7. Academic/Sociological Research
8. Fraud Deterrence (Indicator of anomalies)
Issues with Opinion and Exit Polls in India
1. The "Bandwagon Effect": Polls can influence undecided voters to "join the winner," distorting free
choice.
2. Sampling Errors: Eg. Many 2024 polls used samples of <0.1% of the electorate, leading to significant
seat-projection misses.
3. Media Sensationalism: Channels often present "raw data" as "final seats" to increase TRPs, causing
public confusion.

### [Smash Mains Source Page 155](pages/mains/mains_page_155.pdf)

4. Lack of Transparency: Most agencies do not disclose their methodology, weighting, or funding
sources.
5. Stock Market Volatility: Premature or inaccurate exit polls lead to massive fluctuations in the
sensex/nifty.
6. "Paid Polls" Risk: Potential for political parties to fund "biased polls" to demoralize opposition cadres.
7. Complexity of Multi-Phase Elections: Exit polls for Phase 1 can indirectly influence voters in Phase 7 if
leaked.
8. Voter Fatigue: Constant polling and "doorstep surveys" lead to voter irritation and dishonest responses.
9. Inadequate Rural Representation: "Urban Bias" in sample collection.
Way Forward
1. Mandate agencies to publish sample size, margin of error, and funding alongside results.
2. Empower ECI to audit the methodologies of polling agencies to ensure scientific rigor.
3. Rules to prevent "insider trading" based on advance knowledge of exit poll data.
4. Establish a Professional Body for Pollsters (like the AAPOR in the USA) to set ethical codes.
5. Voter Literacy: ECI campaigns to educate voters that polls are predictions, not results.
6. Encourage University-led polling (like CSDS-Lokniti) which is traditionally more transparent.
7. Digital Watermarking of "official" poll graphics to prevent the spread of fake/edited polls.
Disqualification of candidates
Grounds for Disqualification under RPA, 1951
1. Conviction for Specific Offenses (Section 8):
2. Corrupt Practices (Section 8A)
3. Dismissal for Corruption (Section 9)
4. Government Contracts (Section 9A)
5. Failure to Lodge Election Expenses (Section 10A)
6. False Affidavit (Section 125A)
Grounds for Declaring an Election Void (Section 100) by HC
1. Lack of Qualification (Sec 100(1)(a)): On the date of the election, the candidate was not qualified or was
disqualified under the Constitution or the RPA.
2. Corrupt Practices (Sec 100(1)(b)): Any corrupt practice (as defined in Section 123) was committed by the
candidate, their election agent, or any other person with their consent. Eg. Bribery, undue influence, or
appealing to religion/caste.
3. Improper Rejection (Sec 100(1)(c)): Any nomination was improperly rejected by the Returning Officer.
4. Materially Affected Result (Sec 100(1)(d)): The result was "materially affected" by:
a. Improper acceptance of any nomination.
b. Corrupt practices by an agent (without the candidate's consent).
c. Improper reception or refusal of any vote.
d. Non-compliance with the Constitution or the Act/Rules.
Procedure for Disqualification
1. At the Nomination Stage:
a. Scrutiny (Section 36): The Returning Officer (RO) examines nomination papers. If the candidate is
disqualified under the Constitution or RPA, the RO rejects the nomination.
2. For Sitting Members:

a. Immediate Disqualification: Per the Lily Thomas (2013) judgment, any member convicted for 2+
years stands disqualified immediately, without the 3-month grace period previously allowed.
b. Constitutional Authority: The final decision rests with the President (for MPs) or the Governor (for
MLAs), who must act as per the mandatory advice of the Election Commission (Articles 103 and 192).
3. Election Petition (Section 80): A post-election procedure where a voter or candidate challenges the
result in the High Court within 45 days.
a. Who can file? A candidate or any elector of the constituency can challenge the election.
b. Trial Procedure (Section 86-87):
c. The High Court must endeavor to conclude the trial within six months.
d. The High Court has the power to dismiss a petition summarily if it does not comply with the
provisions of the Act (Eg. failure to join necessary parties).
Examples of Election Petitions:
- Mamata Banerjee (2021), filed an election petition in the Calcutta High Court challenging the results of
the Nandigram Assembly election.
- Allahabad High Court invalidated Indira Gandhi's election from Rae Bareli due to allegations of
corruption.
- Congress leader C P Joshi filed an election petition after losing the 2008 Rajasthan Assembly election
by a single vote.
Remedial Measures Available
1. Stay on Conviction (Not just Sentence):
a. To stop or reverse an automatic disqualification under Section 8, the candidate must obtain a stay on
the conviction from an appellate court.
b. Eg. In 2023, the Supreme Court stayed the conviction of Rahul Gandhi in a defamation case, which
subsequently restored his Lok Sabha membership.
2. Election Petition against RO's Decision: If a nomination is rejected, the candidate cannot immediately
go to court due to Article 329(b). They can file an Election Petition in HC after the election (Section 80)
within 45 days. If successful, the election of the winner is declared void, and a by-election may be
ordered.
3. Appeals (Section 116A): Decisions of the High Court on election petitions can be appealed to the
Supreme Court within 30 days.
4. Power of the Election Commission (Section 11):
a. The ECI has the power to remove or reduce the period of disqualification (except for those
disqualified under Section 8A for corrupt practices).
b. Eg. The ECI reduced the disqualification period of a former Sikkim Chief Minister to allow him to
contest elections.
5. Representation to the ECI (Section 10A cases): If disqualified for failing to file expense accounts, the
candidate can apply to the ECI for a "removal of disqualification" by showing "sufficient reason" for the
delay or failure.
Challenges Related to Legislative Disqualification:
1. Low Conviction Rate: The conviction rate for MPs/MLAs is only 6%.
2. Ambiguity in Grounds for Disqualification

### [Smash Mains Source Page 157](pages/mains/mains_page_157.pdf)

a. Multiple Sources of Disqualification: Articles 102 and 191 of the Constitution, the Representation of
the People Act, 1951, and the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law). This multiplicity often leads to
confusion and interpretational disputes.
b. Vague definition of corrupt practices (Sec. 123) leads to inconsistent rulings.
c. Ambiguity in the office of profit causes arbitrary disqualifications. Eg. Delhi (2018): 20 AAP MLAs
disqualified, later reinstated.
3. Legal and Constitutional Loopholes
a. No Interim Measures: There's no provision to suspend a legislator's functions pending the outcome
of disqualification proceedings.
b. Conflict of Roles: The dual role of political and constitutional actors (like the Speaker or Governor)
creates conflicts of interest.
4. Loopholes in anti-defection law
a. Delays in decisions
b. Political bias of the Speaker
5. Judicial delays prolong uncertainty in representation. Eg. Shiv Sena case pending since 2022
Recommendations for the Future:
Law Commission of India
1. 244th Report (2014):
a. Disqualify candidates at the stage of framing of charges (serious offences with ≥5 years
punishment).
b. Exempt cases where charges are filed within 1 year before elections to prevent misuse.
c. Mandate fast-track courts to conclude trials of legislators within a year.
d. Introduce stricter penalties for false affidavits, including criminal penalties (≥2 years).
2. 255th Report (2015):
a. Shift decision-making on defection from Speaker to President/Governor, acting on Election
Commission's advice.
b. Suggested repealing the merger clause (two-thirds provision).
Election Commission of India
1. Advocates charge-sheet-based disqualification for serious criminal offences.
2. Endorses binding time limits for decision-making on disqualification matters.
Parliamentary & Other Committees
1. Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990): Delete provisions allowing group defections.
2. NCRWC (2002):
a. Suggests independent tribunals for adjudicating disqualification.
b. Recommends constructive vote of no confidence to maintain stability.
3. 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC, 2007):
a. Anti-defection law should apply only to votes impacting government survival.
b. Define ambiguous terms like "office of profit" and "voluntarily give up membership."
SC Judgments Related to Disqualification:
- Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013): Struck down Section 8(4) of RPA, making disqualification
immediate upon a 2+ year conviction.
- Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992): Declared the Speaker a "Tribunal" for defection cases, making
their decisions subject to Judicial Review.

- Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India (2018): Directed Parliament to legislate to bar criminals
from contesting; mandated candidates to publicize criminal antecedents.
- Abhiram Singh v. C.D. Commachen (2017): Held that appealing for votes based on religion or caste is a

Party System
According to Edmund Burke, "Political parties are a group of people sharing common ideology and coming
together for the pursuit of common interest."
"Parties are organized opinions." - Benjamin Disraeli
- There are total 6 national and 67 state parties
- Registered Unrecognized (RUPPs) - over 2500
- Communist Party of India (CPI), Nationalist Congress Party (NCP), and All India Trinamool Congress
(AITC) lost their National status in 2023
- In August 2025, the ECI delisted 334 Registered Unrecognized Political Parties for failing to meet basic
compliance, such as contesting elections or providing updated addresses.
Evolution:
Recognition of political parties
Criteria for Recognition as a National Party
1. Four-State Rule: The party is recognized as a "State Party" in at least four states.
2. Performance in Lok Sabha & Assembly: The party wins at least 6% of the total valid votes in any four or
more states in a General Election (Lok Sabha or State Assembly) AND, in addition, it wins at least four
seats in the Lok Sabha from any state or states.
3. Three-State Lok Sabha Rule: The party wins at least 2% of the total seats in the Lok Sabha (11 seats out
of 543), and these members are elected from at least three different states.
160

---

### [Smash Mains Source Page 159](pages/mains/mains_page_159.pdf)

Criteria for Recognition as a State Party
1. The party secures at least 6% of the valid votes polled in the State Legislative Assembly election AND
wins at least two seats in that Assembly.
2. The party secures at least 6% of the valid votes polled in the state during a Lok Sabha General Election
AND wins at least one seat in the Lok Sabha from that state.
3. The party wins at least 3% of the total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly OR at least three
seats in the Assembly, whichever is more.
4. The party wins at least one seat in the Lok Sabha for every 25 seats (or any fraction thereof) allotted to
that state.
5. If a party fails to win any seats but secures at least 8% of the total valid votes polled in the state (either
in Lok Sabha or Assembly elections), it is eligible for State Party status.
Key Benefits of Recognition
1. Exclusive Symbols: National parties have a reserved symbol used across India. State parties have a
reserved symbol for use within that specific state.
2. Free Airtime: free broadcast time on Akashvani (AIR) and Doordarshan during elections.
3. Electoral Rolls: Recognized parties receive two free copies of the electoral rolls.
4. Star Campaigners: They are allowed up to 40 star campaigners (unrecognized parties get only 20),
whose travel expenses are not added to the candidate's election budget.
5. Eligible for government land/bungalows for party headquarters at subsidized rates.
Significance of the Party System in a Democracy
1. Institutionalization of Political Competition (Sartori)
2. Act as a link Between State and Citizens, ensuring participation and pluralism.
3. Simplifies Political Choice (Duverger) - simplify voter decisions by organizing ideologies and candidates
under identifiable labels. Eg. BJP's hindutva vs. Congress's secularism
4. Collective accountability - Voters can reward or punish parties in government. Eg. Voters punished UPA
in 2014 for corruption issues.
5. Promotes Political Socialization (David Easton) - Eg. Youth wings like NSUI, ABVP train future leaders.
6. Aggregates and Articulates Interests - Almond & Verba (Civic Culture) - Parties convert diverse interests
into coherent policies in their manifesto.
7. Provides a legitimate channel for dissent through organized opposition in Parliament.
8. Institutionalized party systems ensure predictable competition and government stability.
9. Representation of Diversity - Parties allow minorities and regions to participate through inclusive,
coalition-based politics.
10. Samuel Huntington (Political Order Theory) - Parties channel social conflicts into legitimate political
competition, preventing instability.
11. Facilitates Peaceful Transfer of Power - Party competition provides a stable mechanism for leadership
change without violence.
Issues with Party System in India:
1. Rise of Personality-Driven and Dynastic Politics - Eg. RJD, DMK.
2. Criminalization of Politics - As per ADR, 46% of sitting Lok Sabha MPs face criminal charges, with 31%
involving serious offences like murder, attempt to murder, and rape.
3. Weak Intra-Party Democracy - Most parties lack internal elections, policy debates, or grassroots
involvement. Eg. high command culture
161

---

### [Smash Mains Source Page 160](pages/mains/mains_page_160.pdf)

4. Lack of Transparency in Candidate Selection - opaque ticket distribution processes favor wealthy,
connected, or loyal candidates over capable ones.
5. Defections - Eg. "Horse trading" during floor tests or Rajya Sabha elections.
6. Regionalization and Fragmentation - Proliferation of regional parties has led to coalition politics and
policy paralysis. Eg. UPA-II
7. Decline of Mass-Based Party Structures
a. Christophe Jaffrelot highlights the decline of ideology-driven mass movements and rise of
electoral machines.
b. Many parties are no longer rooted in social movements or worker participation (Eg. decline of CPI(M)
cadre model).
8. Frequent suspensions, limited speaking time, and surveillance have weakened the deliberative function
of opposition parties.
9. Yogendra Yadav - identity-based mobilization (caste, religion, region) has overtaken program-based
politics.
10. Erosion of Party Ideologies due to rise of catch all parties. Eg. cash transfer policies by both BJP and
Congress
11. Opportunistic pre-poll or post-poll alliances without common minimum programs. Eg. The Maha
Vikas Aghadi (MVA) alliance in Maharashtra
12. Freebies Culture - distribution state resources in exchange for loyalty, creating systems of patron-client
relations. (Atul Kohli) Eg. Ladli behna scheme
Political Parties under RTI
In 2013, CIC declared six national parties as "public authorities" under Section 2(h) of the RTI Act as they
receive indirect government funding (land at concessional rates, tax exemptions, free airtime).
Political parties have consistently refused to comply, arguing they are not "public authorities." They have
not appointed Public Information Officers (PIOs) as required.
A PIL filed by ADR and Ashwini Upadhyay is currently pending in the Supreme Court.
Arguments in favour
1. Financial Transparency: Citizens can track the exact source of funding, including small donations
currently hidden under the ₹20,000 threshold.
2. Institutionalizing Parties: RTI encourages parties to maintain better records, professionalizing their
internal administration.
3. Curbing Corruption: Eg. Scrutiny of funds could prevent the "Crony Capitalism".
4. Informed Electorate: allows voters to judge party's true intent and democratic functioning
5. Public trust increases when selection criteria for candidates are made transparent.
6. Checks on Criminalization: RTI could reveal the internal deliberations for fielding candidates with
criminal backgrounds.
7. Public Accountability: Parties enjoy 100% tax exemption under Section 13A of the IT Act. RTI ensures
this public subsidy is audited.
8. Reducing Black Money: Transparency forces parties to move away from cash-heavy transactions to
digital, traceable formats.
9. Global Alignment: It brings India in line with advanced democracies like Germany and the UK, where
party finances are public.
162

---

### [Smash Mains Source Page 161](pages/mains/mains_page_161.pdf)

10. Foreign Contributions: need for transparency to prevent external influence on policies.
11. Legal Safeguards: Section 8(1) of the RTI Act ensures sensitive information remains protected, balancing
transparency with confidentiality for political parties.
Arguments Against
1. Political Vendetta: Parties fear that rivals will use "frivolous" RTI queries to stall their functioning
2. Strategic Secrecy: Disclosure of "strategy meetings" or alliance talks could compromise a party's
competitive edge.
3. Privacy of Donors: Fear of harassment by the ruling party can discourage donors.
4. Conflict with Free Speech: Parties argue they are voluntary associations protected under Article 19(1)(c).
5. Administrative Burden: Most parties lack the infrastructure to handle the volume of RTI applications.
6. Disclosure of internal deliberations on "ticket distribution" could lead to internal rebellions.
Way forward
1. Enact a separate "Political Party Transparency Law" to bring parties under RTI ambit. Restrict the RTI
scope to:
a. Financial disclosures (donations, expenditure, electoral bonds)
b. Organizational details (internal elections, constitution, office-bearers)
c. Public resource usage (land, subsidies, free airtime)
2. Mandate Annual Transparency Reports on funding, and decision-making processes
3. Empower ECI to audit party accounts through CAG-approved auditors. (Venkatachaliah Commission)
4. Digital Transparency: Mandate real-time disclosure of all donations over ₹2,000 on party websites.
5. Global Best Practice (Germany): Parties receive state funding only if they follow strict transparency and
internal democracy laws.
Intra-party democracy
Intra-party democracy refers to the practice of democracy within political parties, ensuring that
decision-making is carried out in a transparent, participatory, and accountable manner by party members.
Presently, there is no statutory backing for internal democratic regulation of political parties in India and the
only governing provision is under Section 29A of the Representation of the Peoples' Act, 1951 (dealing with
registration of political parties).
Key Features
1. Regular internal elections for leadership posts.
2. Transparent candidate selection for elections.
3. Inclusive decision-making through debates and consultations.
4. Accountability of leadership to party members.
5. Protection of dissent and internal criticism.
Significance:
1. Prevents Hero Worship - As Dr. B.R. Ambedkar stated, "In politics, Bhakti or hero worship is a sure road
to degradation and eventual dictatorship."
2. Reducing Criminalization in Politics
3. Strengthens Internal Accountability- Ensures party leaders remain answerable to members
4. Prevents Dynastic Politics and Concentration of Power (High Command Culture)
163

---

### [Smash Mains Source Page 162](pages/mains/mains_page_162.pdf)

5. Promotes Transparency and Openness- Eg. collective protest by group of 23, or the G 23 led to
presidential polls in Congress
6. Improves Candidate Selection- merit-based nominations instead of nepotism or favoritism.
7. Enhances Representation- Provides space for youth, women, and marginalized groups.
8. Encourages Policy Responsiveness as Party decisions reflect grassroots opinions
9. Prevention of Defections as leaders as loyal to party
Issues:
1. Weak Role of Election Commission- Though parties must submit constitutions under Section 29A of
RPA, 1951, the ECI lacks enforcement power to ensure genuine internal democracy.
2. Lack of Internal Elections- Most parties avoid regular internal elections or conduct them superficially
to show compliance.
3. Local leadership determined by dominant caste rather than democratic voting.
4. Dynastic Politics - Eg. Congress, Samajwadi Party, DMK, RJD, Shiv Sena etc.
5. Centralisation of Power in the hands of a few top leaders; grassroots members have little say.
6. Absence of Transparency in Party finances, candidate selection, and policy decisions.
7. Weak Institutional Structures- Many parties lack internal mechanisms like disciplinary committees,
grievance redressal forums, or decision-making councils.
8. Suppression of Dissent- Members who question leadership face expulsion or marginalisation.
9. Money and Muscle Power skews candidate selection and internal decisions.
10. Personality Cult Politics reduces collective decision-making and accountability.
Way Forward:
1. Amend RPA 1951: Give ECI the statutory power to deregister parties that fail to hold genuine internal
elections.
2. Law Commission (170th Report): Recommended a legal framework to ensure mandatory internal
democracy and financial transparency.
3. Link state funding of elections to the practice of internal democracy by parties. (Indrajit Gupta
Committee)
4. The "Primary" System (USA): Adopt a model where party supporters (not just leaders) vote to select
their election candidates.
5. Independent Audit: Empower the CAG or a neutral body to audit the membership rolls and election
records of political parties.
6. Grievance Redressal: Establish a "Party Ombudsman"—an independent internal body to hear
complaints from disgruntled party workers.
Coalition Government
Coalition governments are formed when no single political party secures an absolute majority in the
parliament, leading to the need for two or more political parties to come together to form a government.
Types
1. Minority Coalition Governments: Eg. V.P. Singh Government (1989-1990), P.V. Narasimha Rao
Government (1991-1996)
2. Majority Coalition Governments: Eg. United Progressive Alliance (2004-2014), National Democratic
Alliance (2014-present)
164

1. Alliance of Multiple Parties
2. Common Minimum Programme
3. Power Sharing Arrangement
4. Collective Decision-Making
5. Consensus-Based Governance
6. Political Instability
7. Checks and Balances
8. Frequent Renegotiations
9. Enhanced Representation

Benefits of Coalition Governments
1. Promotes power sharing -Prevents one-party dominance by distributing power among allies.
2. Encourages consensus-based governance -Policies require joint approval from partners, ensuring
balance. Eg. MGNREGA.
3. Represents diverse interests -Includes regional and social groups in decision-making. Eg. DMK and

4. Strengthens federalism -Gives regional parties a voice in central policies.
5. Prevents authoritarianism -Limits concentration of power in one party or leader.
6. Promotes political moderation -Partners with differing ideologies adopt moderate policies.
7. Increases democratic participation -Involves multiple parties, enhancing representation. Eg. NDA has
more than 20 Parties
8. Promotes issue-based politics - Eg. Common Minimum Programme under UPA-I emphasized social
welfare.
9. Facilitates inclusive governance -Minorities and smaller groups get policy representation.
10. Encourages negotiation and cooperation -Develops political culture of dialogue and compromise.
11. Reflects true electoral mandate -Mirrors the multi-party choices of Indian voters.

Challenges of Coalition Governments
1. Policy Paralysis: Ideological differences can stall decision-making.
2. Instability: Coalitions can be fragile and prone to collapse. Eg. Frequent changes in government in 1990s
3. Compromise on Ideologies: Eg. BJP and PDP's coalition in Jammu and Kashmir
4. Corruption and Opportunism: Eg. scams like 2G scan, Coal Scam during UPA.
5. Fragmented Governance - Different coalition partners may control different ministries, leading to lack
of coherence and coordination in governance.
6. Populism and Short-Term Focus - Coalition partners may push for populist measures to appease their
voter bases, focusing on short-term gains rather than long-term planning.
Way Forward
1. Institutionalize Pre-Poll Alliances with clear agendas and power-sharing agreements.
2. Legal Framework for Coalition Ethics - Formulate a Coalition Code of Conduct defining roles,
responsibilities, and conflict-resolution mechanisms.
3. Adopt a Common Minimum Programme (CMP) - Formalize a written CMP to guide coalition policy and
reduce ideological clashes.
4. Create joint coordination bodies for dispute resolution and regular consultation.
5. Promote Intra-party and Inter-party Democracy
6. Ensure Transparency in Coalition Agreements - Make coalition terms public to enhance accountability
and voter trust.
7. Political Consensus on National Issues - Build cross-party consensus on critical national policies (Eg.
national security, economic reforms).
- Election Commission of India - Proposed a "Coalition Conduct Charter" and stronger enforcement
powers for the ECI to handle alliance-related violations.
- Germany - Coalition partners sign a formal coalition agreement detailing policy priorities, portfolios,
and dispute mechanisms.
- Netherlands - Governments formed based on Coalition Accords, which are public documents ensuring
transparency and accountability.
Electoral Funding
Political funding refers to the methods used by political parties and candidates to raise money for their
activities and election campaigns.
Key Data Points
1. ADR 2025-26 report - Total donations (above Rs 20,000) to National parties rose by 161% to Rs 6,648
crore. (Over 91% of the total went to BJP)
2. Corporate houses account for over 92.18% of the "declared" donations to national parties.
3. BSP declared zero donations above Rs 20,000 for 19th year.
4. Rising Election Costs: Estimates for the 2024 General Elections put the total expenditure at over ₹1
lakh crore (approx. $12 billion)
5. "Unknown" Sources: Despite reforms, nearly over 65% of regional party incomes still come from
"unknown sources" (donations below ₹20,000), according to ADR reports.
